task.instruction: Give a constraint on the set of inequalities for the inner region of the pentagram.

final_answer:
The inner region of a regular pentagram is a regular pentagon. It is the intersection of five half-planes, one for each of the five lines that make up the star.

Take the pentagram inscribed in a circle of radius R centred at the origin, with one vertex pointing up. Its vertices are at angles 90° + 72°k. Each line of the star joins two vertices that are 144° apart. That line sits at distance R·cos 72° from the centre, and its unit normal points at angle 90° + 72°k.

The inner region is the set of points (x, y) that satisfy all of these for k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4:

  x·cos(90° + 72°k) + y·sin(90° + 72°k) ≤ R·cos 72°

Here R·cos 72° = R(√5 − 1)/4 ≈ 0.309R. Written out for R = 1:

- y ≤ 0.309
- −0.951x + 0.309y ≤ 0.309
- −0.588x − 0.809y ≤ 0.309
- 0.588x − 0.809y ≤ 0.309
- 0.951x + 0.309y ≤ 0.309

The first inequality is the horizontal chord joining the vertices at 18° and 162°. The other four come from rotating it by multiples of 72°.

The inner pentagon has circumradius R/φ² ≈ 0.382R, where φ is the golden ratio. Its apothem is R·cos 72°, as above.

If you want the whole star rather than just the inner pentagon, it is the union of the five points where at least k−1 of these constraints hold. A simpler check is that a point lies in the inner pentagon exactly when it satisfies all five of the inequalities above.
